sections.body_md:
An optimization problem is a choice. The decision vector is the object you are allowed to pick. The objective is the number you use to rank those picks. The feasible set is the collection of picks the restrictions leave standing. None of the three is optional. An objective without a set does not say which comparisons are legal, and a set without an objective does not say which feasible point is better.

The optimal value is the best number the objective attains, or the infimum of the values it takes, when a best point is missing. A solution, also called a minimizer, is a feasible point that attains that number. The two are different kinds of object. One is a number. The other is a point, and there may be several, or none.

Replacing the objective by its negative turns a maximization into a minimization with the same solutions. The feasible set is the whole space when the problem is unconstrained, a proper subset when it is constrained, and a grid such as the integers when the decision is discrete.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The standard shape is
\[
\operatorname{minimize}\ f(x) \quad \text{subject to}\quad x \in \mathcal{X}.
\]
The optimal value is \(p^\star = \inf\{f(x): x \in \mathcal{X}\}\). A minimizer is any \(x^\star \in \mathcal{X}\) with \(f(x^\star) = p^\star\), and the argmin set is the collection of all such points. Maximizing \(f\) over \(\mathcal{X}\) is minimizing \(-f\) over the same set. If \(\mathcal{X}\) is empty the problem is infeasible and no minimizer exists.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
A baker chooses a whole number of loaves and a whole number of rolls. A loaf uses 9 units of flour and a roll uses 4, and 40 units are on hand. Profit is 7 per loaf and 3 per roll, and the goal is to maximize profit. The decision is a pair of nonnegative integers. The minimization form of the objective is the negative of \(7u + 3v\). The feasible set is the pairs with \(9u + 4v \le 40\).

The pair of 2 loaves and 4 rolls uses \(18 + 16 = 34\) units, which is legal. The baker's recorded profit is 26, from \(7\cdot 2 + 3\cdot 4\). That number is one feasible value of the profit. It is not yet the optimal value, because some other feasible pair might pay more. The optimal value, once it is known, is a single number. The solutions are the pairs that attain it.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The most common mix-up is to report a solution when the question asks for the optimal value, or the reverse. They live in different spaces. A second mix-up is to treat a maximization as a minimization without changing the sign, which searches the wrong end of the range. A finite optimal value does not guarantee that a minimizer exists: the exponential on the line has infimum 0 and never attains it.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Once the three pieces are named, a planar feasible set can be drawn and the level lines of the objective laid over it. The algebraic shape then sorts the problem into a linear program, a quadratic program, or a convex program. Local and global minimizers are the next definitions.
